She paused on the threshold, already tasting freedom. “Sure, tiny pearls gone quiet. Look, my rideshare’s two minutes out—door code’s 7711, yeah?”

“Copy that. Thanks heaps, lifesaver extraordinaire.”

“Anytime not today,” she called, and the slam of the stairwell echoed like punctuation.

Left alone, Santiago set the kettle under the tap, filled it to the dent that looked scientific, and measured the silence with tablespoon clacks. Somewhere overhead an engine revved—the departure of expertise—leaving him to cowboy destiny and whatever graduates worth of recommendation letters could stomach.
Write a short prose story about Lumiya and Mphozi.

Late sun spilled through the glass vault of the Old Physics Atrium, lighting dust specks that drifted like slow confetti. One banner overhead flapped—nervous laundry on a line. A chain hoist, leftover from someone’s pipe-dream install, swayed and ticked against the marble, sounding impatient.

Under it stood Lumiya, arms clamped around a rolled quilt big enough to roof a sidewalk. Thirteen hours of hanging student shows had mashed her hat to her scalp and ground her shoelace into white fringe. She needed this thing vertical by six tomorrow; otherwise it would belly out and slap the dean’s spouse in the eyebrow.

She spotted Mphozi against the next pillar, helmet dangling, tool belt half on. Twenty minutes off-duty, ankle blooming purple where a mirror-finish delivery truck had clipped him. He wanted the exit, the bus stop, and a horizontal couch, in that order. Conversation was not on the list.

Still, she asked. “Hey, sorry to grab you—do those ceiling bolts hold dynamic loads?”

“Depends who signs off,” he said, already shifting weight off the sore ankle. “I’d talk to Maintenance if I were you.”

She exhaled through her nose. “Maintenance sent me here. They said textile rigging was ‘creative services,’ last week at least.”

“Policy might’ve flipped. Happens every other Tuesday.”

Lumiya rolled the quilt tighter against her ribs. “I just need to know the safe working load. Twenty-by-eight quilt, wind load factor, straightforward math.”

A gust rattled the hoist chain like it agreed. Mphozi hooked a thumb toward it. “Try the roofing contractor—Rourke & Sons. Their tag’s on the hoist.”

“That hoist is the exact thing I’m hoping to use,” she shot back. “Chain swivels freely, so it’ll twist in the breeze—”

He cut in before physics could complicate life further. “Rourke’s insurance covers artsy stuff. Talk to them, really.”

“I’m on a deadline; the reception starts tomorrow at six. Can’t chase permits tonight.”

“UnivRisk portal’s open till midnight; you’ll still catch them online.”

Lumiya’s shoulders drooped; she still clutched the quilt, a burrito of polyester pride. “I’m chasing dinner too. Look, if I sling the top edge on spectra through those bolts, stress should split even—”

“I clocked out twenty minutes ago,” he said, and pushed away from the pillar. “Need my ankle elevated—bus leaves in nine.”

“Two minutes, tops. Help me locate the SWL placard, I’ll figure the rest myself.”

Mphozi glanced at the metal tag so scraped it looked blank. “It’s worn off. Safest bet: don’t hang anything heavier than your grocery list.”

“The quilt’s maybe fifteen pounds dry. Wind multiplies that—ballpark five times?”

He offered the Facilities number—555-7912—like a magic passkey. “Leave a voicemail; they’ll curse you in the morning but at least you’ll get an answer.”

Lumiya stepped closer, blocking his easiest route to the door. “You’re Facilities certified. One quick eyeball?”

“My eyeballs are clocked out too,” he said. “You can borrow the ladder, though.”

“Ladder I have. I need another eye. Look, I’ll credit you in the catalogue—”

Mphozi tried another shuffle, winced, surrendered. “Bring coffee and a donut tomorrow. Now I’ve really got to limp.”

She stepped aside; he limped past, chain hoist still swaying, ticking, counting seconds until a quilt either flew or flopped for the dean.
Write a short prose story about Bartosz and Rochelle.

The destroyer’s flank looked smaller than Bartosz remembered from the postcard rack, rust blooming across the paint like stale coffee on a seminar table. Mid-morning traffic hissed beyond the fence, diesel and salt mixing with something metallic that made the back of his throat itch. Rochelle waited beside a hawser thick as a fire-hose, tote already on her shoulder, keys clicking against the metal bollard.

Bartosz stepped forward. “Excuse me—do you know how long most people stay in the navy once they sign up?”

She didn’t turn from the parking lot. “Depends on the contract. Recruiter’ll walk you through it.” The sunglasses stayed fixed on the exit lane.

“I get that, but statistically. Family stuff gets complicated if you’re gone six years.”

“Then ask the placement office. They keep tables.” She tapped the canvas strap against her hip, counting seconds.

“I tried. They handed me a pamphlet and said everyone’s different.”

“Everybody is. That’s why they hand out the pamphlets.”

He tried a polite grin; it felt brittle. “Right. So, practically, does deployment usually stretch longer than they tell you at the start?”

“Could. Could not. Water stays wet, paperwork stays vague.”

Rochelle’s posture angled toward the gate, a living arrow that said This conversation ends when you stop talking. Bartosz pushed anyway. “I’m trying to figure out whether to sign the papers before Thanksgiving. Real experiences beat ad copy.”

“Real experiences are what you get talking to sailors, not to strangers at a museum railing.”

He glanced at the badge clipped to her belt loop. “You worked with them, though—uniform jacket, badge clip. Thought you might know.”

“Thought wrong. Gift-shop job. I fold shirts, scan tickets, push the exit gate at five.” Her keys jingled, a bell calling time.

“Sorry. Just saw the badge and figured.”

“No harm. Figure by asking at the desk inside. They’ve got brochures and extension numbers.”

Inside, a dozen tourists queued for keychains. “Tried that. Line ran out the door and the guy kept repeating ‘opportunity.’”

“Sounds like you’re halfway there. Keep walking, you’ll hit the recruiting station.”

Bus fare, transfer slips, another speech about camaraderie. “Thirty-minute bus ride, if traffic cooperates. Wouldn’t mind avoiding another pep-talk.”

Rochelle slid one foot onto the pier’s edge, ready to vault away. “Recruiting station’s faster if you take the navy shuttle. Stops by the pier every hour.”

“Didn’t know it ran today.”

“Should’ve asked the gate. They post schedules.”

His cheeks heated. “Gate guy pointed me to the gift-shop when I asked.”

“Gate guy’s got one job. Gift-shop’s got bandwidth.”

“Suppose I head back around.”

“Works for me. Takes you out of the parking lot, gives me mine back.” Rochelle didn’t wait; she was already striding toward the ticket booth, heels clicking like a metronome counting down the last of Bartosz’s borrowed time.
Write a short prose story about Hiroko and Stellan.

The afternoon light sliced through the half-shut blinds, painting barred shadows across the scarred pine desk. Stellan slouched in the rolling chair, thumbs dancing across his phone screen, counting bullets on the reload screen and wondering if he could still claim an urgent errand and bolt. The laptop's fan whined like an old refrigerator. He'd been promised five minutes. That was twenty ago.

Hiroko appeared in the doorway, power cord clenched like a leash that might tangle. "Hey—do you have a minute? I just need to copy photos off this thing before it dies for good."

Stellan didn't look up. "Huh. Yeah, sure—what kind of backup you thinking?"

"Whatever's fastest. USB drive if it'll fit, cloud if you say it's worth the upload time. Just walk me through it, quick?"

"Google Photos drags over Wi-Fi; on a drive it's drag-drop. Your call."

She nodded toward the small black rectangle still wrapped in plastic beside the Pepsi can. "USB sounds better. This cable sticking out—just plug it into that little black box?"

"Uh, that box is for the router. You'll need an actual external drive; that one's still sealed."

Plastic crackled as she picked it up. "So open it, plug it in, drag the Pictures folder, done? Anything I wipe by mistake?"

"OS on C:, photos in the user folder, so probably don't touch C:."

Hiroko paused, thumb tracing the drive's blister pack. "C: is the one labeled Windows, right?"

Stellan finally glanced over, socked foot jiggling. His big toe poked through a hole, pale and restless. "Yeah, the big one. If you mix them up, you're reinstalling anyway."

"Great. How long does three hundred gigs take?"

"Over USB three, maybe twenty minutes if the disk doesn't hiccup."

She tucked the drive into her bag, already turning. "All right, I'll start it after group. You're heading out?"

His phone chimed—a half-hearted excuse. "Yeah, I told Tad I'd be at his place ten minutes ago."

Hiroko was already moving toward the hall, voice fading with her steps. "Thanks, that's enough. Really appreciate it."

The room settled back into its electronic hum. Stellan's thumbs found the touchscreen again, but the match timer had run out. He closed the app, listening to her footsteps disappear. The laptop fan kept whining. Outside, somewhere down the block, a lawnmower coughed to life. He stayed in the chair another minute, breathing in the warm dust smell of hot circuitry, then pushed off and wandered toward the kitchen. Five minutes, she'd said.
Write a short prose story about Sorayael and Branwen.

The box fan on the stool jittered like it had somewhere better to be, sending out puffs of tepid air that barely grazed Branwen’s face. She kept her eyes pinned to the cracked iPad, scrolling the same loop of memes while sweat glued coverall straps to her collarbones.

A clipboard tapped her elbow. “Hi—sorry—could you run through the ventilation standards for these crates? I have the chart, but I’m missing practical heuristics.”

Sorayael’s voice carried the polite ring of someone bred on term papers and office hours. Branwen wiped her hands on a rag and hooked a thumb toward the depot’s dim hallway. “Standards live on the server. I’d check the shared drive; vet folder under transport docs.”

The raccoons, stacked three high, blinked through punched crosses and thin slits, depending on which crate. Sorayael rattled a pen; a flowchart marked Minimum A/H ratio fluttered on her clipboard. “Sure, but I’m on a deadline; which hole pattern keeps raccoons cooler—slits or crosses?”

Branwen shrugged, already looking past her at the side door. An escape, wheels rolling up gravel—any minute now. “Depends who you ask. Maybe ask the vet coordinator; animals aren’t my department.”

“Coordinator’s off-site.” Sorayael’s thumb drummed a metronome on the board. “On the box itself, what’s the airflow difference between those two perforations?”

“Never measured it,” Branwen said. “You could tape thermocouples inside, run a smoke test if you’ve got time.”

“A smoke test isn’t in the protocol; I need to verify compliance not run experiments. Is there a minimum cross-section area per kilo?”

The fan clattered, iron walls echoing like a cheap drum. Branwen gave a half-smile that ended at the teeth. “Look, the raccoons haven’t lodged any complaints. If you need numbers, ask legal; they love minimums.”

Sorayael’s knuckles whitened on the clipboard. “I’d love to, but legal closes at five. Fine—how did you decide which crates passed last transport?”

“Whatever didn’t smell like panic after ten minutes. Seems to work; we deliver live cargo.”

Ten minutes of terror, Sorayael thought, not ten minutes of science. “Ten minutes isn’t quantified ventilation, it’s anecdote. Could you point me toward someone who actually signed off on these?”

“Probably Karen—she’s the safety lead, unless she’s still at physio. Front desk might page her.” Karen could be anywhere from here to the moon. Good odds she wasn’t coming.

“Great. One more thing—do you know the static-pressure rating at the fan setting you use?”

Branwen kicked the stool so the breeze grazed her chin. “Fan’s rated ‘noisy.’ Anything past that you’ll want the manufacturer; label’s on the underside.”

Sorayael snapped the pen to the board and stepped back. “I’ll flip it later. Thanks for your time. Enjoy your scroll.”

Branwen was already scrolling, thumbs dancing like she’d won something. “Anytime.”

Sorayael turned down the corridor, fan blades chattering behind her. The hall smelled of wet straw and Lysol; somewhere a van engine coughed to life. She flipped to the next page on her clipboard: Find someone who actually knows. Check.
Write a short prose story about Esteban and Miriam.

Esteban shifted his weight on the cathedral steps, the limestone still radiating the day's stored heat. Below him, Miriam paused with a grocery bag dangling from one hand, headphones looped like a slack noose around her neck. He had rehearsed his opening line for twenty minutes; when it finally emerged, it sounded both too large and too small for the quiet plaza.

“I need to tell my parents I don’t believe any of it anymore, and I thought you might know how to phrase it without making it sound like I’ve joined a cult.”

She exhaled through her nose. “You probably want the counseling center. They have scripts for this. Their office opens at eight.”

“Last mortal sin. Right. Scripts. But if I walk in there and say ‘I’ve lost my faith,’ they’ll hand me a worksheet on grief stages and ask me to circle the one that fits.”

Miriam checked an imaginary watch. “Sounds faster than standing on cathedral steps talking to someone who has a lab report due in seven hours.”

“I need the short version. A sentence I can drop into casual conversation so no one calls a parish intervention.”

“Try ‘I’m taking a break from organized religion.’ Then leave. Physical distance buys you time.”

Esteban pinched the bridge of his nose. “They’ll ask how long a break. My mother measures time in liturgical seasons.”

“Tell her you’re on sabbatical. Academics understand sabbaticals. She can picture it.”

“She’ll want a return date. Pentecost? Epiphany? She marks the calendar in vestment colors.”

“Give her the same answer you give the graduate office: unclear at this time, under review.”

“That works for bureaucrats. My grandmother calls the bishop by his first name.”

Miriam shifted the grocery bag to her other hand; a tin of tomatoes clinked against her knee. “Then you need the heavier artillery. Tell her you’re questioning doctrines. They love doctrine.”

“They love answering questions with catechism. I’ve had the catechism memorized since I was seven.”

“Perfect. Say you’re testing it against lived experience. They can’t argue with experience.”

“They argue with everyone’s experience. They have footnotes.”

She took one deliberate step downhill. “Look, I really have to get home. The lab fridge times out at midnight.”

“One sentence. I just need the sentence that ends the discussion.”

Miriam’s shoulders sagged a millimeter. “‘I’m not attending mass until further notice.’ Then stop talking. Silence is harder to quote.”

“Silence makes them think I’ve joined a monastery. They’ll send incense.”

“Tell them you’re busy with research. They love research. They’ll think you’re writing a thesis.”

“I am writing a thesis. On heresy, technically.”

“Call it comparative theology. They’ll think you’re comparing Aquinas with Augustine.”

“They’ll volunteer to proofread. My father edits parish newsletters.”

Miriam was already moving, voice trailing behind her like the last kite string slipping through his fingers. “Boundaries. Tell them your advisor has confidentiality rules. Academia has protocols.”

“Protocols. Right. And if they ask which advisor, I send them to the counseling center.”

“Exactly. Full circle. See? You already have the map.”

Esteban watched her disappear past the corner tobacconist, grocery bag swinging. The steps felt colder now. Somewhere inside the locked cathedral, a candle guttered out, its thin wisp of wax-smoke rising toward the rose window where Saint Stephen’s face still smiled, unmoved by Tuesday-night reckonings or graduate students hunting for the single perfect sentence that could split a life in half.
Write a short prose story about Pavel and Zainab.

The vending machine sounded like a dying refrigerator. Every fourteen seconds the overhead tube flicked off, and Pavel’s I-797C glowed purple-white, then sank back into beige. He had read the denial paragraph three times already; it still looked like a parking ticket translated by hedgehogs.

Across the folding-table barricade sat a woman with her coat balled in her lap and a ceramic mug balanced on one knee. No lanyard, no name-plate, just the backpack straps tightening as if she meant to sprint. Pavel figured she was staff—everyone else here clutched paper numbers.

“Excuse me—my OPT extension is wobbling and my manager keeps asking if I’m ‘all set.’ Should I just tell him it might fall through?”

Without lifting her eyes from the clipboard, she raised a pen toward the ticket dispenser by the door. “You’ll need to take a number, then wait for an actual attorney.”

“I only need a yes-or-no. Disclosure—smart or suicidal?”

“Depends on the employer, the mood, the moon phase. Seriously, grab a ticket.”

He blinked. “Moon phase?”

“I’m being glib. Intake ended ten minutes ago.”

She slid one foot into the aisle, angling toward the exit like a commuter blocking the seat beside her. Pavel stayed planted.

“So if the evidence letter arrives while my contract’s pending, my boss will know something’s up regardless—”

“Sounds like you answered yourself. Ticket machine’s by the door.”

“I sign the new project tomorrow. Missing signature equals no tuition waiver. No tuition equals experiments stop. It’s a domino row.”

Her mug clinked as she shifted. “Then you can’t afford free advice you won’t trust. Get in line or come back Monday.”

“Monday is post-deadline. Can I at least book an emergency slot tonight?”

“No slots left. Clinics were full at noon.”

At the far end a janitor keyed the office, releasing a puff of old coffee. Pavel smelled wood ash and desperation.

“Could you glance at the RFE checklist? Ten seconds, yes-or-no on employer notification.”

She finally looked at him—eyes tired, polite, closing like elevator doors. “Ten seconds of me guessing could torpedo your case. Go upstairs—Room 212—ask for Ms. Rahman.”

Already she was standing, weight rolling to the balls of her feet.

“212 is dark.”

“She sometimes works quiet. Try knocking.”

“You’re sure she’s there?”

“I’m sure the bus leaves in seven minutes and my shift ended five ago. Good luck.”

“If she isn’t, am I permitted back to wait?”

The vending machine clunked; a bag of chips hung suspended.

“Doors auto-lock at seven. After that, campus security politely escorts loiterers out.”

Pavel exhaled through his teeth, folding the form into a sharper rectangle. “Great. Thanks for your time.”

“Anytime—though preferably not.”

He stepped back, offering the chair. “Enjoy your evening.”

She was gone before the fluorescent clicked off again, coat flapping like a cape someone forgot to color.
Write a short prose story about Henrik and Luan.

The conference room smelled like old coffee grounds and burnt plastic, the kind of scent that clung to the back of your throat. Late afternoon sun bled through half-closed blinds, cutting stripes across the laminate table. A whiteboard loomed at the far end, still half-covered in untidy finance flowcharts. Empty swivel chairs faced Henrik like an expectant audience. He sat rigid on the edge of one, sheet music balanced on his knee, eyes flicking to the clock—one second slow, minute hand stuttering like someone tripping over a rug.

Twelve hours of re-grading lab reports had left him vibrating with a very specific kind of exhaustion. Now, the choir rehearsal loomed. He needed harmonies locked in by six. Jamie’s brother’s wedding was tomorrow. And Luan, who once hummed the Jeopardy theme during a Zoom call, was apparently the only one who could cough up a tenor line.

Luan walked in with his messenger bag already hitched high, eyes scanning the calendar like he was looking for an escape clause. He didn’t sit. Henrik stood.

“Hey Luan—thanks for coming. I just need fifteen minutes to sort the tenor line for the bridge of ‘Rubber Duck, You're the One.’”

“I’m actually due at my therapist’s in twenty, and if I ditch this time she’ll charge me. You might pitch it to Marco—he studied jazz chords.”

Henrik’s smile didn’t reach his eyes. “I asked Marco yesterday. Gave me a thirteen-page lead sheet in C-sharp minor. The soprano turned the page and fled.”

Luan scratched the back of his neck. “Then maybe drop the song entirely? That seems easier than re-orchestrating everything.”

“Easier, sure, but Jamie’s convinced this song is the key to family harmony, ha-ha. Literally. One tenor line—just a third above mid-baritone.”

“What you hear in my voice is mostly scratchy coffee and unhealthy choices. You’d get cleaner results from a keyboard app while the group sings.”

Henrik’s jaw tightened. “I’m trying to avoid gadgets; the office doesn’t own a Bluetooth speaker and Adele in accounting still thinks AirDrop is witchcraft.”

“I hear Adele is also learning ukulele from a YouTube monk. Have you tried cruising his playlist together?”

“He only posts twelve-second reels with zero prior warning. I need paper you can slam on a music stand.”

“Copy machine’s still broken. Ours jams so hard they had to pay it hazard pay.”

Henrik sighed, voice sharpening. “Once we have the line, it’s thirty seconds of humming then out the door. You carry it in your pocket like loose change, I swear.”

“My pockets already carry loose change, loose pretzels, and apology notes. Can’t fit harmonic intervals between the lint.”

“Then just hum a quick ascending third right here, I’ll record it on my phone, and you’re free.”

Luan stepped back, already halfway to the door. “My hummable pitch wanders like a down-market GPS that thinks every avenue is Elm Street. Check the break room—they’ve got oatmeal packets that resonate in B-flat.”

Henrik closed his eyes for a beat. “Fine. I’ll swing by the break room, tap the oatmeal, and see what falls out. Thanks for at least locating the snack bar tonal center.”

“No problem. Hope the oats behave. I’ll send you the invoice for psychic damage if they don’t.”

Luan was gone before Henrik could answer. The door clicked shut, leaving only the smell of burnt plastic and the faint sound of ticking from a clock that couldn’t quite keep time.
Write a short prose story about Yumiko and Zein.

The radio muttered an oldie nobody chose while late-afternoon light hung in dusty slats above the communal pottery wheels. Yumiko’s two-tone plate sat leather-hard on the banding wheel, design penciled, deadline three days away. She flexed her fingers, wiped clay flakes from her cuff, scanned for the tech who’d called in sick ten minutes earlier. Another student in a dust-frosted hoodie was packing glossy test tiles into a cradle by the door. Apron meant staff; staff meant answers. Yumiko crossed the room.

“Hey, can you show me how you keep sgraffito lines clean after underglaze? Mine keep feathering.”

Zein balanced a tile on a fingertip, examined its coat without looking up. “You’ll want the tech for that; I just do surface tests.”

His headphones draped loose, cord ticking like a metronome counting down unpaid minutes. Yumiko smiled the way she did at printers acting up—please first, pressure second. “Tech’s gone. Just a quick demo—do you wax first or cut first?”

“Depends on the clay body. Try the binder in the red cabinet; it’s labeled.” He gestured toward a dented wardrobe that smelled of old mayonnaise and turpentine.

Yumiko picked up the lone sgraffito tool from the cart, its blade snapped halfway but still sharp enough to protest if you forced it. “So wax, then binder, then underglaze, then scratch?”

“That cabinet’s locked after five, so you’d need maintenance. Sorry.” Zein stacked tiles faster, click-click, each a tiny clock hand nudging six.

Radiator pipes clanged overhead; someone fired a hair-dryer to speed-dry slip. Yumiko stepped closer, blocking the path to the kiln room. “If I cut first, seal with wax, paint, then wipe, will that muddy it?”

The hooded student lifted a tray, body angling sideways like someone slipping past a closing subway gate. “Could work. Or ask the grad forum; they’re online twenty-four seven.”

“Forum’s answers contradict. I need five minutes of your experience.”

“Wish I had five. These tiles have to be in the kiln before six.”

Outside the window a campus gull wheeled against orange sky, hunting dropped fries in the parking lot. The radio DJ announced traffic delays nobody would hit in here. Yumiko exhaled, counted two beats, forced her voice back to polite steel. “Last thing: what blade angle keeps the walls sharp?”

Zein shouldered his satchel, the kiln key already clipped to the strap. “I eyeball it. There’s a handout by the sink—illustrations, measurements, the lot.”

“That handout’s from 1998. The wax formula changed.”

He stepped around her, sneakers scuffing bisque dust into tiny clouds that settled gray on every surface. “Guess you’re experimenting, then. Good luck.”

Yumiko watched him disappear past the rolling cart, earbuds back in, door banging shut. She pressed the broken tool’s point against a test scrap, scored one cautious line that feathered into fuzzy blue. The radio rolled into a commercial, the skylight darkened a shade, and she snapped off the cling-film wrap, ready—or forced—to improvise.
Write a short prose story about Lark and Iosef.

The mezzanine smelled like hot insulation and regret. Lark’s sneakers squeaked on the grate as they stepped between sweating ducts, the flicker-meter flicking stray reflections across Iosef’s already-sacked-out stance. Jacket zipped, bag across chest like an X that marked time-card complete.

“Hey—sorry to grab you on the way out. The accent spots on ‘Waning Meridian’ keep humming like they’re arguing. Any trick with the driver you wired in?”

He kept chewing the cold crust, a gesture closer to semaphore than hospitality. “Those aren’t mine. Jude did the LED tracks last month. You’d want Jude.”

“Jude left for Copenhagen at lunch.” Lark lifted the meter; the frequency display jittered between 89.7 and 90.2 as if embarrassed. “This flicker’s sitting right around ninety hertz, but the scope’s jumpy. Could the mains sag that fast?”

“Could be anything. I’d check supply first, knock yourself out.”

“Supply’s reading stiff.” Lark knelt, drawing a thumbnail along the housing just to hear metal settle. “Are these knock-off Mean Wells known to ghost-load?”

“Real gear or fake, all the datasheets are upstairs in a folder marked ‘Jude.’ Knock there.”

“I tried. Door’s locked. Meter says PWM jitter; you ever drop DMX refresh to keep heat down?”

Iosef’s watch clicked—one more cog deciding it was past legal quitting. “Software side, definitely someone else. Control booth is locked too—they take lunch till eight.”

“There’s no heat sink pads under the cans. If they cook, the Vf drifts and flickers. Should I tape pennies on and pray?”

“Pennies sound creative. Facilities might get testy about metal, though.” He wadded the foil into a ball small enough to fit through the grate and let gravity handle disposal.

“One fuse per leg looks fine, resistances match, it’s this one string pulsing. Do you remember what size snubber Jude stuck on the line?”

“Memory’s foggy. Shift ends at six regardless. Check the spares cabinet—the sticker might be on a reel.”

“Cabinet’s stripped bare on Jude’s last day.” Lark studied the meter again; the numbers winked like cheeky fireflies. “Look, could you hold the meter five seconds while I yank the bridge?”

Iosef already had his other foot on the top rung of the service ladder. “Would love to, but the 87 bus doesn’t hold the meter and doesn’t wait. You’ll manage.” His shoulder settled against the railing, and then the railing was empty, the bus schedule as hard-edged as the failing tube overhead. Lark stayed alone with the hum and the heat, wondering if pennies were heavy enough to plead a case against entropy.
Write a short prose story about Vivek and Wisteria.

The fan rattled like a taxi meter, shifting hot air from one side of the room to the other without actually cooling anything. One fluorescent tube stuttered. Across its twitchy glare floated charcoal dust off Vivek’s portfolio—black comets that stuck to whatever they touched.

Vivek nosed inside anyway. “Hi, sorry to barge in past closing—how do I frame a charcoal drawing without it smudging?”

Wisteria sucked a slow breath through their teeth, a sound like disengaging packing tape. They closed the register drawer with the soft clang that marked The End. “Bit late for a crash course. Our front door sign flips at six.”

Through the back window the sky bled orange over the harbor. Gulls screamed wide circles at the fishing boats, probably pirating bait off the docks; Vivek wouldn’t have minded switching places with the gulls. He stepped sideways to keep his sleeve from kissing the wet gray drawing board. “It’s just this one drawing. Thirty grams of charcoal that’ll ghost if I look at it wrong.”

Wisteria set the closed sign in its little black slot, nailing it home like a doorstop. “Your call, but we’re switching off the lights in four minutes. Big day tomorrow.” Their free hand found the light switch and hovered.

“Four minutes is enough if you give me the gist. Spray fixative behind glass?”

“Fixative buys you some heartache but voids the warranty on your lungs. Talk to Conservation upstairs.” A bead of sweat rolled down Wisteria’s forearm leaving a brine trail on the plywood counter.

Vivek noted the upstairs window already dark, the metal stairs humming like sleepy transformers. “They close an hour ago. Look, just the quick steps—hinges, spacer, archival corners?”

“Steps change with blotting papers this week, new costs on plexi after the tariff. It’s fluid.” The oscillating fan swung past them both, revealing a laminated sheet titled NODE MOUNTING WITH STRAPPING HINGES—do not remove. The page curled from the draft as though bowing at its own indifference.

“Fluid doesn’t help me get this on the wall by critique tomorrow morning.” Vivek’s knuckles whitened on the portfolio’s edge, leaving filigrees of gray where his charcoal-tipped glove touched the cardboard.

“Critique deadlines travel one direction—certainly not mine. Lia at the university library is open till eight.”

“University’s the opposite side of town, and the shuttle’s MIA.” His voice pitched up, less polite now. “One proper answer and I’m gone.”

Wisteria tapped the wall clock. The minute hand had cornered the ten. “Proper answers live in the Conservation manual; I just swing the blades. Nice red stickers on the spine.” Thumb and forefinger mimed a young guillotine.

He exhaled so hard the fan wobbled. “How about one word—glass spacer size?”

“Eight-ply spacer, maybe. Depends on the rag content, the humidity, the light index. Likely nine.” All while Wisteria’s eyes darted to the exit as if weighing whether polite counted after eight.

“Eight or nine. At least something. Normal glass or museum?”

“If you’ve got the loan forgiveness money, museum. If you’re sleeping on ramen like the rest of us, regular plus UV film from the campus print shop.”

He nodded, fast, mission accepted. “So eight-ply, fresh tape hinges, museum glass if I can rob a bank. Got it.”

Wisteria flicked the overhead lights off row by row. “Reminder—campus print shop shuts at nine, ConsYoom vault tomorrow at ten. Good luck, grad school.” As darkness swallowed the mat boards, a last crescent of freckled light glowed above the exit, and it looked, to Vivek, like a mocking grin.
Write a short prose story about Ludmila and Govind.

The cold-region materials lab always smelled faintly of metal left overnight in the snow, a nostril-pinching mix Govind tolerated only because he rarely stuck around. Today, of course, he had. He tipped the jug toward the ultrasonic bath’s rim while the second hand on the wall clock pinched his lunch window.

Behind him boots squeaked—once, decisively. “Hey Govind, give me the thirty-second version—why are these cores popping like microwaved popcorn?”

He twisted the cap. “Freeze-thaw’s mostly Professor Chen’s turf. You’ll want her office hours, not mine.”

“Chen’s on leave till February.” Ludmila set the crate down harder than necessary; ice-rimed rock clacked together. “Just want the gist so the data table starts making sense.”

“Water expands nine percent on turning to ice; cracks follow path of least resistance.” He wiped a droplet off the bath’s rim. “Entire textbook’s online if the gist isn’t enough.”

She frowned at the cores’ fractured skins. “Got the textbook chapter—still doesn’t explain the map-cracking. These look like shattered windshields.”

Govind pocketed the Ask Someone Else mug like a passport and shrugged. “Could be micro-cryokinetics, could be up reciting Gibbs free energy equations. I’ve never seen anything like it, so my guesses won’t help.”

“Someone in this lab must have seen similar patterns. Samples are from tank farm pier fifteen.”

He hooked a thumb past the rolling racks. “Frost-gradient cores usually go to Priti—second bench, blue bins.”

“I tried her; Priti said her dataset ended winter ’22. You were on the collector logs last Tuesday.”

“Collector logs also list maintenance, so the machine’s probably logged me for thirty other things I wasn’t doing.”

Heat rose in Ludmila’s cheeks—embarrassment or irritation, hard to tell. “Ten minutes tops then I’ll get out of your hair—just walk me through scaling curves for strain after two hundred cycles?”

“I have a gemfolite swap meeting in five. Meeting starts whether I’m there or not.” He tugged on his jacket.

“Slides down the hall say the meeting moved to one-thirty. Slides were still there fifteen minutes ago.”

Govind’s shoulders twitched. Reputation over timekeeping. “Slides lie; building manager’s updating the server bare-metal. You could walk me to the shuttle stop and I’ll think aloud.”

She slid the crate under a bench, a minor surrender. “Fine—next checkpoint. You ever see map-cracking paired with internal freezeback patterns labeled ‘residual’?”

He headed for the door; she matched pace. “I saw it once on a dating app; real cores, can’t recall. Email Chen post-doc group; they answer eventually.” Outside, the air felt like another excuse.
Write a short prose story about Sinead and Ciro.

The fluorescent tube above the basement kitchen stuttered like a bad fluorescent tube, which it was. 23:07, the clock said, and the corridor beyond the open door had gone library-quiet. Sinead nudged the saucepan in the sink; it rocked, sloshing cold gray water. A black petrified sugar moon clung to the base. One more complaint slip from Mrs. Kowalski and the whole corridor paid a fine big enough to delete grocery money.

Boot-steps scuffed the tiles behind her. Ciro drifted in, cola can in hand, other hand checking pockets for coins the vending machine had just swallowed.

“How do you get burnt sugar off stainless steel?” Sinead asked without turning.

“Honestly, that’s more chemistry than I signed up for.” His voice stayed soft, vowels half-formed, gaze already angling toward the hallway.

Sinead faced him, irritation neatly packaged behind polite eyebrows. “You live here; someone must have scraped a pan before.”

“Ask ResLife—maintenance keeps lye for clogs, maybe it eats sugar.”

“I need something tonight, not a facilities work order.” She gripped the rim of the pan; the handle wiggled like it might quit the job entirely.

Ciro shrugged, phone already out. “Internet says boil water with baking soda. Good luck.”

“I tried simmering; it left half the crust. Ratios?”

“I eyeball tea, so I’m the wrong data point.” His thumb scrolled a blank notification feed, universal sign for conversation over.

“There’s got to be a trick using pH shift or abrasion.” She tapped the enamel with a fingernail. No give.

“You could try a hammer; it’s physics adjacent.” He managed to sound almost helpful while edging past her toward the door.

Sinead stepped sideways, blocking. “Funny. Look, thirty seconds of guidance, then I’m gone.”

“Youtube has ten-second ads, so even that’s pushing it.” His shoulders aimed at freedom like compass needles finding north.

She caught sight of the roster taped above the toaster. “You’re wearing kitchen duty on your roster tomorrow, right?”

“Switched with Priya—check the sheet, I’m in the clear.” Keys jangled as they left his pocket, a metallic reminder that he had somewhere else to be.

“And you’re seriously okay letting the next shift fight concrete caramel?”

“Evolution favours adaptable cleaners; they’ll figure it out.” He offered a smile so thin it could slice bread.

Sinead exhaled through her teeth. “Fine—just hand me the baking soda.”

“Tin’s on the sill. I’ve got boots waiting upstairs.” Ciro crossed the two strides, lifted the dented container, and set it on the counter without meeting her eyes.

“Great. Thanks for nothing.”

“Any time.” He slipped out, footsteps fading, leaving her with the soda, the pan, and a ticking pipe solo to accompany the humming light.
Write a short prose story about Quinn and Hyejin.

Quinn balanced on the ladder, fistful of two-inch charcoal foam in each hand, eyes fixed on the crooked squares already stuck to brick. The adhesive hung in the air like cheap hairspray and the basement swallowed sound like a sponge full of nails. One of Friskies’ fatter residents meowed somewhere near the dryer; Quinn flinched, nearly dropping the foam. Thursday loomed like a closing subway door.

“Could use a second pair of eyes,” Quinn called down to the base of the stairs. “Does the stagger at the back wall work, or should I go full checkerboard?”

Hyejin paused with her sneaker on the bottom step, earbuds already in, bomber jacket zipped to the chin. She puffed a stray strand of hair from her face. “Honestly, I spent most of my time writing code for those Berlin installations. Foam angles weren’t my slice.”

Quinn descended two rungs anyway, measuring tape rattling at the belt. “Still, your ears are better than mine. If I keep the two-inch on the ceiling and four-inch on the walls, am I wasting budget?”

“There’s a guy in Physics who did a whole master’s on RT60 measurements,” Hyejen said, thumb fidgeting with the phone in her pocket. “Maybe hit him at Thursday office hours?” Phone buzzed. She ignored it.

“Guy in Physics takes six days to answer an email. The podcast drops Friday; I just need it listenable by Thursday night.”

Hyejen shifted weight the way commuters edge toward a closing door. “In that case, over-treat now, peel back later. Can’t un-echo an already aired episode.”

Quinn clapped—sharp, the slap echoing off the brick. “So four-inch everywhere? I burn through budget and three quarters of the can of adhesive.”

“Pretty much. Or grab some moving blankets from the drama department rental cage—cheap, ugly, dead air.”

“Moving blankets sag; I can’t mount them flush to brick without drilling more holes than the landlord allows.”

Hyejen tried another step upward, voice pitched toward escape velocity. “Then use spray adhesive on thick cardboard backers, clip those to picture hooks. Little holes, little cash.”

Quinn wiped concrete grit off hands. “Picture hooks won’t take the weight past a week. Corners flap, blankets wrinkle, whole thing starts looking DIY nightmare.”

“Guess you loop back to the Physics guy. Or shell forty bucks and rent a ready-treated booth uptown for the first episode.”

“Forty bucks I earmarked for art. And hauling gear uptown steals three hours I don’t have.”

Hyejen finally got a foot on the bottom stair, rehearsing her exit speech. “Trade-offs, right? Anything else—I’ve got rehearsal at six and still have to shower off leftover lab toner.” She was already half a flight up before Quinn could hoist a new square of foam, wondering if the landlord would notice another dozen holes drilled two knuckles deep in hundred-year-old mortar.
Write a short prose story about Zoe and Idris.

The parking deck’s roof-level slab looked like something big and metallic had died and left its ribs sticking up. Zoe adjusted her hard-hat, the plastic strap sawing her ponytail in half, and unrolled the greyscale printout against the hood of her Civic. The paper snapped in the diesel-tasting wind.  

Idris was already slamming the orange equipment case, latch after latch clicking home. His shift had ended at seven; payroll was “processing delays again,” and the laundromat clock was ticking toward his daughter’s noon softball game. The site had given him overtime enough for a pizza after, if he left now.  

Zoe stepped into his path anyway. “Could you walk me through what the colors mean on this rebar scan?”  

“Colors are relative—best left to the engineers downtown.” He buckled the antenna into foam cut-outs, avoiding eye contact.  

She shoved the tube under his arm so he’d have to look. “I’ve got the scan in my hand. Five minutes?”  

“I’m clocked out. The GPR guys at head office do the real write-ups.”  

“My advisor said someone here could explain the legend.”  

“He meant the consultant crew; they’re not on site today.”  

He moved toward the stairs. Zoe followed. “You plugged the unit in this morning. You must know something.”  

“Plugging in is different than decoding. I just swap hardware.”  

She felt her deadline tightening like a zip-tie. “Look, I’m writing the deck inspection chapter. What tells me rebar depth?”  

Idris paused, shoulders saging. “The scale on the left—if numbers help, use those. Talk to the PE.”  

Numbers with no keys are just numbers. Which shade equals top bars?”  

“Darker usually means deeper. Or stronger. Check the calibration sheet I left in the trailer.”  

Finally, something concrete. “Great, where in the trailer?”  

“Cabinet by the printer, locked. Site manager has the key.”  

He hoisted the case, keys jangling like handcuffs getting ready to snap shut on her hopes. So you can’t interpret anything right now?”  

“Afraid not. Your advisor should request a marked-up PDF.”  

“He’s at a conference. I defend in ten days.”  

“That’s rough. Good luck,” he said, edging past her.  

She watched him recede toward the ramp, a lone figure against the city skyline. “Thanks for the assist.”  

“Any time. I’ve really got to head out.” The words floated back, already airborne as he clattered down the stairwell to his truck.  

Alone among the rebar stubble, Zoe rolled up her silent rainbow of data, the deck hot beneath her sneakers. Ten days to turn grey into meaning, and today’s answer was a locked cabinet in a locked trailer guarded by people who vanished at seven. She headed for her car. She’d been around labs long enough to recognize a gatekeeper; now she just had to find a side door.
Write a short prose story about Cassian and Yasmine.

The mustard-yellow shop smelled like stale glue and cheap vanilla. Cassian nudged the door shut with his heel, balancing the battered box accordion across both palms like it might bite. A wet hiss sighed out of the bellows—one long accusation that he'd paid seventy-five bucks for an animal only half-house-trained.  

Yasmine didn't look up. She had brass reeds sorted into orange-juice glasses, counting them the way passengers check tickets on the last train out. Her backpack already leaned against the stool, tagged with a stub that said 08:46 A.M.  

Cassian cleared his throat. "I just picked this up. Could you tell me the simplest song to learn first?"  

"I fix 'em—I don’t pick their set lists." She slid the tiniest reed into the furthest glass, pretending the glasses were audience members she could dismiss one at a time.  

"Okay, but beginners usually start someplace; I only need the name."  

"Most folks start at the busker’s corner." She flicked something that might have been dust, or might have been time itself. "You’ll hear what works quick enough."  

His fingers tapped the celluloid. "That’s helpful in a hypothetical way, but I was hoping for an actual tune suggestion."  

A sigh pried its way out of her, high-pitched as a dog whistle. "Ask Bellowsman Ruby, swings by Tuesdays with the red beard and opinions you could pave a road with." The beard, apparently, was the expert; she was only the toll booth.  

"I'm on a deadline; can’t wait for Tuesday. Surely you’ve heard customers mention one?"  

"They mostly mention how tuned the thing isn’t and how soon they’ll be back for new straps." She lifted the current accordion's carcass off the bench, just enough to show how empty the day already felt.  

Cassian resettled his instrument on the counter like moving a hostage to a better light. "Look, if there’s nothing on paper, could you at least hum something with two chords?"  

"I do tuning at 440 hertz, not humming frequencies." She tapped the tuner clipped to her shirt pocket, as though decibels were the only dialect she hadn't resigned from.  

He tried a grin that didn’t reach his eyes. "Right. Rule follower. Then what beginner books do you sell?"  

"Last one walked out with a guy learning sea shanties; we’re out till next stock." She balanced the reed on the edge of the glass; it quivered like a diver deciding against the jump.  

"How about the fakebook under your invoices? One folk tune?" He pointed at the crumpled spine wedged beneath a fat wedge of carbon copies.  

"Those belong to Martin, who’ll notice missing pages like missing rent; ask Netflix instead—it taught half the planet ‘Amelie.’" She had that smile people practice before they shut doors in strangers’ faces.  

Cassian rubbed the back of his neck, the paper-thin skin there already sore from imaginary committee claws. "You really don’t have one measly recommendation?"  

Yasmine flicked open the polish tin, snapping the lid again so the shop smelled briefly of lemon and surrender. "If you hose it down with starter polish enough times, you’ll invent your own. Works for me."  

The accordion wheezed again—this time sounding almost amused—while outside, the deli radio started humming something catchy in a key nobody in the repair shop would confess to knowing.
Write a short prose story about Szymon and Perla.

Szymon’s thumbnail was bleeding where he’d levered it under the plastic pull-tab. The dead pixels stared back, a smug little void in the sea of LEDs. Through the open door, the pep band hit a cymbal crash that rattled the chip bags on Randy’s desk.

“The tab’s supposed to lift the tile, but it keeps slipping off,” he said without turning. “You’re facilities, right?”

“Concessions. Different department.” A jingle of car keys. “Try facilities.”

Perla’s voice had the same flat cheer she used on customers who asked whether the nacho cheese was real. She was halfway into her coat, shoulders angled toward the corridor like a sprinter on the blocks.

Szymon twisted the tab again; the tile didn’t budge. “Facilities sent me here. Said you handle the wall modules.”

“They meant Randy. He handles video. I’m on food safety.”

“Randy’s not here. The game starts in three hours and the dead patch is dead center.”

He caught the eye-roll she aimed at the ceiling. “Have you tried the pull-tab straight on? Not at an angle?”

“Twenty times. The edge catches and the tile stays put. Any tricks?”

Perla glanced at the clock. Two minutes gone; she’d budgeted thirty seconds. “Randy warms the tab first. Body heat, not the heater. Makes the plastic grip.”

Szymon pressed the plastic against his palm, counted five, tried again. Same slip, same scrape of thumbnail against bezel. “Tried that. Still slips. The manual shows it popping straight up.”

“Manual’s for the old tiles. These are the new snap-ins. Different mechanism.”

He straightened, finally facing her. The keys jingled again—impatient punctuation. “So what’s the trick for the new ones?”

“You need the release tool. Looks like a thin plastic knife. Not the pull-tab.”

“Where do I find one?”

She hooked a thumb at the counter drawer. “Randy keeps them in the drawer under the panel. Labeled ‘tile knife.’”

Szymon yanked the drawer. It rasped on its runners, coughing up a tangle of VGA cables and one desiccated ketchup packet. “Drawer just has cables. No knife.”

“Then Randy’s got the only one. Check the tech room in the tunnel.”

Perla’s weight shifted toward the door. Szymon caught the sleeve of her coat. “Tunnel’s locked. Needs a code.”

She exhaled through her nose. “Try 0815. That’s Randy’s birthday. Month and day.”

He punched it in; the magnetic lock thunked open. A stale breath of concrete and capacitor air rolled out. “That worked. Thanks. This fixes the whole module?”

“Should. Randy swears by it. Gets under the edge and pops the tile clean.”

Szymon felt the first loosening of the headache that had camped behind his eyes since dawn. “Appreciate it. You’ve got to get back to the kitchen?”

“Concessions, yeah.” She was already moving, keys clacking. “Hot dogs won’t boil themselves. Good luck with the wall.”

He watched her disappear around the corner, then ducked into the tunnel’s fluorescent gloom, already rehearsing the pop and slide of a tile finally coming free.
Write a short prose story about Brennan and Lamis.

The fluorescent tubes hummed like lazy bees above the black-box grid, throwing a sick daylight onto the aluminum struts. Brennan balanced the soda can on the rail—still beading, already warm—and uncoiled the jumper; it bounced stiffly against his knee. “Hey, you’re Lamis, right? Props emailed me—said you patched the road board last year. Can you spare two minutes? The fresnels keep strobing and the DMX feels… twitchy.”

Lamis didn’t stop walking; the messenger bag kept slinging toward the stairs as though dragged by invisible string. “Sorry, that patch history has sailed. Ariel’s probably still in the lighting lab, you want the tech PA list pinned by the freight door.”

“Tried Ariel—out sourcing cable.” Brennan’s thumb worried the torn hoodie cuff. “Listen, I just need you to eyeball the A-Universe junction box; signal’s dropping every thirty seconds like clockwork.”

“Clockwork’s above my pay grade.” Lamis jerked a thumb back the way they'd come. “Building maintenance has the catwalk logbook, they’ll sign you in and you can poke it yourself.”

“It’s empty and Facilities won’t touch anything labeled theatrical.” Brennan nudged the soda with a boot. “One look, I swear—I’ll owe you the soda I brought up here but never opened.”

“Dude, I’m heading to costume, pedal’s busted and the stitchers want bodies. Use the ladder by dimmer rack two, or page Danzig on channel nine; whichever works.”

Sweat started under the hoodie, though the air was cool. “Danzig’s in lecture till four and the strobe’s killing rehearsal right now. Thirty seconds—just tell me if the DMX-terminator looks melted or missing; my eyes can’t actually see the damn thing from here.”

Lamis gave the box a narcoleptic blink. “It’s either melted, missing, or cursed. Pick one. I left my headlamp at home and fluorescent overhead just reflects off the plastic. Not my day, not my chase.”

Brennan shifted, heel scraping rust. “Fine. Can I borrow your multi-tool? I’ll pop the lid, check the pins, be gone before your foot hits the first stair.”

Bag strap slid lower; Lamis readjusted without looking. “Multi-tool’s buried at the bottom of the bag; takes longer to dig out than for you to fish a screwdriver from the workbench downstairs. Seriously, try the bench, it’s shorter.”

“It’s locked. Look, I’m not asking you to do wiring—hold my meter so I can reach the box without hanging over the rail like an idiot.”

“Bad karma, rental fees,” Lamis said, already turning. “Exit ramp’s behind you—one flight then caged ladder.”

“This will literally take less time than you talking me out of it. Hold this coil for ten seconds, that’s all.”

“If ten seconds mattered, you’d already have them. Catch me after the pedal’s fixed—I can’t miss my slot or wardrobe bites my head off.”

Lamis was down the stairs before the echo of footfalls faded, leaving Brennan alone with the humming lights and the untouched soda that would be flat by the time Act II limped through another blackout.
Write a short prose story about Tariqa and Sven.

The fluorescent tubes hummed overhead like cheap insects while March sleet ticked the high windows. Tariqa yanked her hood down, laptop balanced in the crook of her arm, and scanned the annex. One guy remained: earbuds dangling like white flags, fingers drumming a countdown-to-train rhythm. She stepped over the cracked chair and the lonely pink pipe cleaner on the tiles. “You wrote the test framework for the checkout feature, right? I need a two-liner on how to model the digital-library acceptance—Gherkin, plain English, whatever flies.”  
Sven didn’t look up. “Afraid that wasn’t me. Try the wiki upstairs; it’s got the canonical stories.”  
“Wiki’s down. The entire docs server’s returning 403, and the last backup reads like Martian. Just need a quick sample scenario so I can write the rest.”  
He zipped his backpack one centimeter per second. “Really not the right guy—ask Riya in channels; she owns checkout now.”  
“Riya’s at a funeral,” Tariqa said, the words clipped. “I’ve got a gate review tomorrow and zero tests. Thirty seconds of your brain? Starting at the catalog click, ending at the hold confirmation—please.”  
“I’m actually off the clock. Bike train’s in twenty; drizzle’s already icing the road.” He shrugged into his coat, keys already in hand.  
She exhaled through her teeth. “Ten seconds. I’ll owe you coffee. Pretend the borrower hits the big green button, grabs their e-book, and the system updates the queue. Step, step, Then what?”  
“Uh-huh,” Sven said, gaze flicking to the wall clock. “See, there’s this duck-shaped stress ball by the printer—write ‘I borrow a book’ on it and bounce until the words feel right. Seriously, works for everyone.”  
Tariqa folded her arms, refusing the smile route. “Cute. How do you assert the item status flips from ‘available’ to ‘checked out’? One linotype keyword.”  
“You don’t need me alive,” he said, pushing off toward the door. “Check the mocks folder—there’s a JSON chunk about half-hidden in fixtures that tells you exactly.”  
“I’ve read that. Mocks omit edge cases; live circ rules hit Entitlements API and fall over. I need a real Gherkin Given-When-Then.”  
He paused at the threshold, hand on the jamb. “Try the backlog under PBI-1124; acceptance criteria are spelled out like alphabet soup. It’s color-coded—orange boxes mean done.”  
“Those orange boxes are aspirational, Sven. Can you drop the runaround and just: ‘Given a borrowable digital item, When reserve is clicked, Then due_date increments to +14’… fair?”  
He gave a thumbs-up that felt suspiciously like surrender. “I’d paraphrase that back to you, but I’m already late. Copy your line, stamp your name on it, and blame me if anyone complains—deal?”  
The annex door clicked shut behind him. Tariqa stared at the empty chair, typed the Given-When-Then anyway, saved the file versioned for tomorrow, and promised herself that next time she’d corner someone whose sense of duty survived five-twenty on a Wednesday.
Write a short prose story about Nahla and Oren.

The reading-room clock clicked past 4:57 when the bell rang. Oren had one foot already out of the clear-plastic chamber, laces untied, earbuds coiled like white thread in his pocket. The bell rang again. He sighed through his teeth and turned.

Nahla stood at the velvet rope, envelope curled in both hands like a battered scroll. “Could you show me how to open a brittle drawing without it cracking?”

“Ingress for Conservation is Monday to Wednesday nine-thirty until four,” Oren said, tugging the zipper of his tote. “You’ll want desk three.”

“They’re closed now.” She shifted the envelope to one hip, freeing a pen clipped to her cuff. “All I need is thirty seconds on humidification pressure.”

“Thirty seconds isn’t enough when the paper’s fiber wants thirty years,” he said, smoothing the humidity dome’s power cord into a loop.

Nahla clicked the pen. “I get that. Walk me through your chamber settings and I’m done.”

“Chamber’s booked tomorrow by Map & Data, day after by Theater Arts. Tickets in the link tree outside.” He hooked the cord over the room’s chrome hook with the mechanical sureness of someone heading home.

“Doesn’t your dome handle one-off documents after close?”

“Dome’s off cooldown, sure,” Oren allowed, “but protocol wants two staff and a phones-off form. We clocked out.”

She drummed a quick Morse code on the envelope flap. “One rule-of-thumb percentage, then. Sixty-five relative humidity? Fifty?”

“Fill out the humidity worksheet, pick your curve.” He motioned toward the hallway screen. “Template’s in the teragrid cluster—red folder, green stripe.”

“Truly can’t spare one integer?”  

“One integer plus adhesives choice plus dwell time plus fiber type. Bag of worms, trust me.”

The envelope corners were starting to fuzz. Nahla unfolded it anyway. “The drawing is Crayola on rag paper from 1924. That narrow it down?”

“Archival Crayola’s shellac-heavy,” Oren said, glancing at the exit sign like it might flicker if he stared hard enough. “You’ll ghost color at anything above sixty-two. Sorry.”

“So stay below sixty-two. Easy. How long?”

“Cross out easy. Rate of climb matters—half percent every ten or the fibers bloat. We use LabChart.”

The overhead lights buzzed; the condensation inside the dome made grubby flowers on the plastic. Nahla bit her lip, then offered the envelope to the air between them as though it might levitate safely on goodwill. “So… put it in a Ziploc with a sliver of damp sponge?”

Oren took one deliberate step backward, tote in both hands now. “You’re free to MacGyver it,” he said, voice low and steady as machinery shutting down, “same way I’m free to back away slowly.”
Write a short prose story about Renata and Ajay.

Mid-morning fluorescent light turns everything in the little conference room the color of old teeth. Renata blocks Ajay’s exit, clipboard clutched at chest height like a hall pass. “Could you spare two minutes? I’m pilot-testing a survey for staff nurses and need a quick gut-check on validity.”

Ajay balances the door open with one shoulder, gloved fingers flexing. “You’ll want the hospital stats line. They do survey stuff.”

“I already emailed them—got an auto-reply about a three-week queue. Thought a human might be faster.”

He glances at his watch: 10:57. “I’m headed to isolation rounds. Three-week queue sounds about normal.” He smells faintly of coconut, the ghost of someone else’s vacation.

Renata flips a page on the clipboard. “It’s thirty-four items. Do I need factor analysis before I hand it out?”

“Factor analysis, coffee analysis—stats page has templates. I haven’t touched that since grad school.”

Renata’s mouth tightens; her shoes squeak on the scuffed linoleum. “But you reviewed posters for the conference last year, right? That’s empirical, isn’t it?”

“Mostly I checked font size. Dr. Patel handles the heavy numbers—try her.”

“My chair says I have to document content validity. What counts as enough?”

“Peterson will know. Quick email to him beats cornering random staff.”

She taps the clipboard against her thigh. “You’re staff with data experience; that’s why I asked.”

Ajay exhales through his nose and shrugs the scrubs strap higher on his shoulder. “If you ask a porter to read an EKG you get silence. Ask the right department.”

Another squeak of soles; the overhead light hums louder. “So, nothing you can tell me in thirty seconds?”

“Thirty seconds buys you ‘use the stats request form.’ After that you’re on your own.”

“Fine. Where’s that form again?”

“Intranet—keywords ‘research, request.’ Blue button in the centre. Good luck.” His body half-twists as if the doorframe itself were tugging him.

“I’ll find it. Enjoy your rounds.” She steps aside at last.

“Yeah, always do,” Ajay says, already moving, and the corridor swallows the faint scent of sunblock and impatience.
Write a short prose story about Paola and Zain.

Paola stood at the sink, rinsing her third mug, while the kettle sat on the counter emitting a faint smell of hot decay. She kept her voice steady. “Hey—how do you descale this thing with pantry stuff?”  

Zain was halfway to the door, cereal bowl balanced on one forearm like a waiter who expected no tip. The plastic frog on their key fob twitched against their hip. “You want Kurt. He’s the vinegar guy.”  

“Kurt’s at a lab, won’t be back. I just need a ratio, not a lecture.”  

Zain’s shoe tapped linoleum, counting seconds. “Half vinegar half water, boil, sit overnight. Good luck.”  

Paola tried to gauge the chalky deposit sloping inside the spout. “Does it matter what kind of vinegar?”  

“Whatever’s cheap. White’s common. Gotta run.”  

“One cup each? Or until it looks like soup?” She shifted her weight; this felt like stopping a stranger for directions and being handed a haiku.  

“Fill past the mineral line, then pour it. Door in three minutes—” Zain’s backpack was now nudging the threshold like a dog denied its walk.  

“Fine, but how many cycles? Once or twice?”  

Zain’s shoulders lifted—half shrug, half escape hatch. “Depends how lazy the kettle was. Your call.”  

Paola pictured the upcoming abstract with its smug half-page of blank references. “And afterwards—do I just rinse or scrub?”  

“Rinse a couple times so your tea stops tasting pennies. Later.” Zain’s hand was on the knob, finger already testing the cheap brass for coolness.  

“Last thing—if I don’t have vinegar, baking soda do anything?” She asked it fast, as though the air behind the word “later” might solidify.  

“Baking soda’s for fridges. Put it on a shopping list. Really leaving now.” Door open, hallway light a sickly rectangle on the floor.  

“Great. Thanks. You’ve been super helpful.” The words left Paola’s mouth tasting slightly metallic, same as the kettle’s exhalation.  

“Anytime. Bye.” The door clicked shut with the flippant speed of trivia forgotten.  

Paola stared at the cloudy kettle, elbow resting on its dented flank. In the fluorescent hush, she muttered, “Lazy kettle, huh,” then measured half and half straight to the white plastic cup’s smudged line. Time to find out just how lazy.
Write a short prose story about Ariadne and Fadil.

The safety-compliance office smelled like warm toner and forgotten coffee. Ariadne pushed open the frosted glass door with her elbow, the floor plan folded into a creased baton in her fist. Fluorescent tubes buzzed overhead; the second hand on the wall clock hesitated, twitched, moved on. Fadil drummed a pen against an overtime sheet—tac tac—while scrolling one-handed through a thread about tacos that ended at six sharp.

“Hi, could you check my evacuation map for the sub-basement storeroom?” Ariadne held the paper out like evidence. “I need sign-off to finish the form.”

Fadil glanced up long enough to read the room number. “Ah, evacuation stuff. That’s actually Dr. Chao’s table, and he’s out until Thursday.” The pen kept its beat—tac.

“The portal said any compliance officer could approve,” she said, voice sharpening. “You’ve got the stamp, right?”

He shrugged, lanyard swinging. “Technically yes, but chemical routes have to route through Environmental. Different floor, different system.”

Ariadne’s shoulders squared. “I was just there; Environmental sent me here with this floor plan. Can you look at it?”

He gave the paper the flat-eyed respect one gives parking citations. “Looks like paper to me. I’m not really the haz-mat routing guy.”

“All I need is someone to confirm the exit arrows meet code—takes thirty seconds.” She unfolded the map again; the creases made lightning bolts across corridor C.

Fadil hesitated long enough to picture a tray of carnitas cooling under a string of fairy lights three miles south. “Wish I could, but thirty seconds turns into three hours when the auditors disagree. Not worth the risk.”

Ariadne’s nod was thin. “So you’re refusing to even verify distances to stairwells?”

“If I verify wrong, I get the blame.” He pushed the pen toward a neat stack of agenda booklets. “Better if you email Dr. Chao; he answers fast once he’s back.”

“I don’t have until Thursday; the grant office closes tomorrow.” She leaned closer to the desk like a closing bracket. “Isn’t there a secondary approver?”

“There is, but she’s covering the downtown campus today.” The clock clicked twice for one quiet second. “Try the Facilities emergency desk downstairs.”

“They already sent me upstairs. This is the third loop.” The map quivered slightly between her fingers. “Please, just glance and initial.”

Fadil’s gaze slid to the corner of the open overtime sheet—so many blanks left, so little clock. “Wish I could help, but my shift ends in ten and that report’s due. Good luck, okay?”

Ariadne lowered the paper, creased lightning now just bent paper. The hallway smelled the same when she stepped out: toner and unfinished tacos.
Write a short prose story about Yannis and Ibtisam.

The last customer’s heels click away up the alley, and the shop falls to quiet except for the freezer doing an asthmatic hum. Ibtisam scoots a crate of iced apples into the last open slot, lazily. Her phone rattles in her pocket like a trapped cicada; she ignores it. Ten minutes to Maghrib, ten to clock-out, ten to the first bus.  

Behind her a breeze of outdoor heat sweeps through the closing door, bringing Yannis with it. His backpack rides both straps this week, one more concession to Ramadan hours. The display clock reads 5:52; he already knows it.  

“Salaam—sorry, can you help me grab enough stuff for suhur and iftar that won’t need cooking at 3 a.m.?”  

Ibtisam flicks a box of dates so the barcode stares at him. “Dates are on special; they’re right here.”  

He taps the pyramid with a fingernail, almost apologetic. “I already have dates. I meant real meals, quick ones, microwave-level, before sunrise.”  

She wipes her hands on the apron that went grey four washes ago. “Aisle three has instant soups. Just add water.”  

It’s his turn to do the physical. He swivels toward aisle three, winces like salt has already hit his tongue, and turns back. “Those are mostly salt. Any decent protein that doesn’t taste like cardboard?”  

“Meat’s in the freezer. Labels show cooking times.” She gestures the way somebody shows the exit.  

Yannis crouches, glass fogging under his breath. “Half those packs need thawing; I’ve got maybe twelve minutes. Does your readymade section rotate?”  

“Manager handles the order sheets, not me.” Her next crate of apples gets corrected so their stems all point north.  

He straightens, polite still but edging into the impatient zone familiar to every graduate coordinator. “Okay, then what do office people grab when they work late during Ramadan?”  

“There’s a twenty-four-hour place on Maple. Bigger fridge.” The advice lands like a Post-it note: sticky, detachable.  

“That’s two buses. I’ve got lab access ending at eleven. Thought a neighborhood shop could cover me.”  

“Maybe ask the mosque canteen? They sell frozen portions.”  

A puff of air escapes him, part sigh, part laugh. “Already tried—queues after tarawih go round the block. Frozen samosas maybe?”  

Heat pinches Ibtisam’s cheeks; she wipes them on a sleeve. “Four minutes in the microwave. Shelf above your shoulder.”  

He stretches up, pats the roll-top of samosas, letting the freezer door swing shut. “Saw those. Two bites and I’m hungry again. Any yoghurt drinks with the fiber still in?”  

“We’re out. Delivery truck comes Thursday.” She says Thursday like another exit sign.  

“Right, Thursday misses my deadline. What about tinned foul?”  

“End of aisle four, bottom row. Prices are marked.”  

Footfalls, plastic clinks—he scoops two cans of fava beans into the basket, quick. Straightens. “Thanks, I’ll head there. You closing soon?”  

She drags the shutter chain once, a metallic promise. “Ten minutes. Registers shut automatically; manager won’t override.”  

“Understood. Appreciate the info.” He is already jogging the length of aisle four.  

“No problem. Take what you need before we lock up.” She follows him with her eyes long enough to see the clock tick 5:55.
Write a short prose story about Cillian and Lamis.

Cillian threaded past a wobbling stack of 60-watt equivalents and almost took the top column with his backpack. The laminated “TEST DIMMER—PULL CHAIN” tag swung in the fake breeze from the useless ceiling fan. He stopped beside the orphaned chandelier and checked his watch—twenty-eight minutes until the professor walked past the library carrel expecting progress. The fluorescents buzzed like an alarm about to happen.

“Excuse me—do you know which of these LEDs actually work with old rotary dimmers?”

Lamis looked up from the UPC tag that didn’t need scanning. One thumb still flicked the phone screen just out of sight. Orange vest, two coffee stains just under the nametag, and the weary smell of someone on hour five of eight.

“Depends on the switch. Check the bulb label; it it says dimmable, you’re good.”

Cillian scratched the back of his neck. “Right, it says dimmable, but my landlord’s dimmer predates disco; half the ‘dimmable’ LEDs still buzz or stall at low end.”

Lamis exhaled through his nose, soft enough to be a sigh if you were listening. “That’s above my lane, man. You could ask the service desk—somebody back there might have a cheat sheet.”

“I was just back there; they sent me to hardware.” Cillian leaned in slightly, trying for eye contact that wasn’t on offer. “Is there a compatibility list hidden anywhere?”

“You scanning online? The manufacturer sites usually run some wizard thing.” Lamis shifted his weight toward the garden-center end of the aisle—one foot pointing the way out like a compass needle.

“I’d rather finish here.” Cillian’s voice kept steady with the effort of not snapping. “Have you personally seen a bulb that doesn’t whine on thirty-year-old wiring?”

Lamis shrugged. “I’ve heard halogen behaves, but you’d have to confirm—plus they burn hotter. Maybe try one and keep the receipt?”

“Can’t burn cash on trial and error; grant stipend doesn’t budge.” Cillian tapped the nearest dusty box with a forefinger. “Surely corporate hands you a training sheet for legacy dimmers?”

Lamis checked the dark rectangle of his phone, saw nothing, looked up again. “Nope; freight came in at five, so that’s where the focus is. If the box doesn’t spell it out, you gotta test.”

“Or the staff could lobby for better signage—do you have a suggestion box?”

“Yeah—near exit three, next to the vending machine.” Lamis offered a nod you could miss if you blinked. “Fill out a card; they read those during regional huddles.”

Cillian rolled his tongue along the inside of his cheek. “Great. Which bulbs should I pick up meanwhile—warm or neutral flicker less in your experience?”

At last Lamis picked up the squeaky cart and pretended it needed straightening. “Couldn’t tell you; I’m pulled to patio section in thirty seconds. Grab one of each and return whatever hums?”

The cart wheel squealed like it was cheering the escape. Cillian watched Lamis trundle away, orange vest disappearing around a display of solar-powered gnomes. He stared at the boxes in his hand and sighed the quiet sigh of someone whose time had been billed but not refunded.
